claim: MPS1 inhibitor reversine treatment for 24 hours increases the frequency of micronuclei in B16F10 cells by >10-fold over the basal level of ~1%.
source: MPS1i increased the frequency of micronuclei visible in interphase cells (Figure 1B), as micronuclei are often used as a surrogate for CIN and genome instability (Cohen-Sharir et al., 2021; Crasta et al., 2012; Harding et al., 2017; Mackenzie et al., 2017). Regardless of the MPS1i concentration, we saw >10-fold increases of micronuclei over the cell line's low basal level (~1% of cells), and two other MPS1i inhibitors AZ3146 and BAY12-17389 confirm such effects (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1B and confirmed with additional inhibitors in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Micronuclei-positive cells can persist up to 12 days after MPS1 inhibitor treatment.
source: Micronuclei-positive cells can persist up to 12 days after treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), while control cells maintain the low basal levels.
evidence: The claim is supported by time-course data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B showing persistence of micronuclei.

claim: 34% of MPS1i-treated B16F10 cells show aneuploidy compared to 10% of DMSO-treated cells as determined by InferCNV analysis.
source: 34% of MPS1i-treated cells show aneuploidy, as determined by InferCNV, compared to 10% of DMSO-treated cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell RNA-sequencing data analyzed with InferCNV pipeline as shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Tumors comprised of MPS1i-treated B16F10 cells show downregulated transcripts for numerous genes encoding M2-like (pro-cancer) macrophage polarization markers at days 5 and 10 post-challenge.
source: Comparison of tumors comprised of MPS1i-treated and DMSO-treated cells by differential gene expression showed distinct downregulated transcripts for numerous genes encoding M2-like (pro-cancer) macrophage polarization markers (Figure 1E). At day 5 post-challenge, classical M2 markers Arg1, Marco, and Cd274 are downregulated, and although several M2 markers are upregulated (Mrc1, Cd163, and C1q complement genes), by day 10, these, Marco, and Cd27 are all downregulated.
evidence: The claim is supported by bulk RNA-sequencing data from whole tumors shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Cytokines Ccl2, Ccl4, Ccl7, Ccl22, and Il21r associated with an M2 phenotype are consistently downregulated in MPS1i-treated tumors at both days 5 and 10.
source: Furthermore, at both days 5 and 10, cytokines Ccl2, Ccl4, Ccl7, Ccl22, and Il21r associated with an M2 phenotype (Cerezo-Wallis et al., 2020) were found to be consistently downregulated.
evidence: The claim is supported by bulk RNA-sequencing data and cites a reference for the M2 phenotype association.

claim: Gene set enrichment analysis revealed that pathways related to DNA damage, cell cycle, and growth are downregulated in tumors comprised of MPS1i-treated B16F10 cells.
source: Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) further revealed that pathways related to DNA damage, cell cycle, and growth were also downregulated (Figure 1F), consistent with previous studies (Cohen-Sharir et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 1F and is consistent with cited previous studies.

claim: BMDMs treated with conditioned media from MPS1i-treated B16F10 cells show increased expression of M1-like anti-cancer markers and little-to-no expression of most M2-like pro-cancer markers.
source: Clusters 0 and 2 that consisted mostly of MPS1i-treated B16F10 secretome showed increased expression of pro-inflammatory, M1-like anti-cancer markers and little-to-no expression of most M2-like, pro-cancer markers (Figure 1I and J).
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell RNA-sequencing data of BMDMs shown in Figure 1I and J.

claim: Early-stage CIN in cancer cells can activate macrophages via secreted factors toward M1-like anti-cancer activity.
source: These results suggest that early-stage CIN in cancer cells can activate macrophages via secreted factors toward M1-like anti-cancer activity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the single-cell RNA-sequencing data of BMDMs treated with conditioned media.

claim: BMDMs from immunotumoroids of MPS1i-treated B16F10 show increased surface expression of M1-like markers MHCII and CD86.
source: Consistent with our whole-tumor bulk RNA-sequencing and also single-cell RNA-sequencing of BMDM monocultures (Figure 1E, I, and J), BMDMs from immunotumoroids of MPS1i-treated B16F10 showed increased surface expression of M1-like markers MHCII and CD86 while showing decreased expression of M2-like markers CD163 and CD206 (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: BMDMs from immunotumoroids of MPS1i-treated B16F10 show decreased expression of M2-like markers CD163 and CD206.
source: Consistent with our whole-tumor bulk RNA-sequencing and also single-cell RNA-sequencing of BMDM monocultures (Figure 1E, I, and J), BMDMs from immunotumoroids of MPS1i-treated B16F10 showed increased surface expression of M1-like markers MHCII and CD86 while showing decreased expression of M2-like markers CD163 and CD206 (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: MPS1i-treated cancer cells show decreased binding of anti-Tyrp1 antibody.
source: Although these macrophages seemed poised for anticancer activity, the cancer cells showed decreased binding of anti-Tyrp1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) and ~20% larger size in flow cytometry (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: MPS1i-treated cancer cells are ~20% larger in size as measured by flow cytometry.
source: Although these macrophages seemed poised for anticancer activity, the cancer cells showed decreased binding of anti-Tyrp1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) and ~20% larger size in flow cytometry (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: CIN-afflicted tumoroids are eliminated by BMDMs regardless of anti-Tyrp1 opsonization.
source: We indeed find CIN-afflicted tumoroids are eliminated by BMDMs regardless of anti-Tyrp1 opsonization (Figure 2D and E), whereas anti-Tyrp1 is required for clearance of DMSO control tumoroids (Figure 2; Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by 3D tumoroid phagocytosis assay data shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: Anti-Tyrp1 is required for clearance of DMSO control tumoroids by BMDMs.
source: We indeed find CIN-afflicted tumoroids are eliminated by BMDMs regardless of anti-Tyrp1 opsonization (Figure 2D and E), whereas anti-Tyrp1 is required for clearance of DMSO control tumoroids (Figure 2; Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by 3D tumoroid phagocytosis assay data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: CIN-afflicted tumors have 3-fold more CD45+ immune cells compared to DMSO controls at day 5 post-challenge.
source: Flow cytometry showed the CIN-afflicted tumors had 3-fold more CD45+ immune cells (Figure 2G – i), 2.5-fold more CD45+ CD11b+ (myeloid) cells (Figure 2G – ii), and an ~6-fold increase in F4/80-positive macrophages (Figure 2G – iii) relative to DMSO controls.
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data from in vivo tumors shown in Figure 2G-i.

claim: CIN-afflicted tumors have 2.5-fold more CD45+ CD11b+ myeloid cells compared to DMSO controls at day 5 post-challenge.
source: Flow cytometry showed the CIN-afflicted tumors had 3-fold more CD45+ immune cells (Figure 2G – i), 2.5-fold more CD45+ CD11b+ (myeloid) cells (Figure 2G – ii), and an ~6-fold increase in F4/80-positive macrophages (Figure 2G – iii) relative to DMSO controls.
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data from in vivo tumors shown in Figure 2G-ii.

claim: CIN-afflicted tumors have ~6-fold increase in F4/80-positive macrophages compared to DMSO controls at day 5 post-challenge.
source: Flow cytometry showed the CIN-afflicted tumors had 3-fold more CD45+ immune cells (Figure 2G – i), 2.5-fold more CD45+ CD11b+ (myeloid) cells (Figure 2G – ii), and an ~6-fold increase in F4/80-positive macrophages (Figure 2G – iii) relative to DMSO controls.
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data from in vivo tumors shown in Figure 2G-iii.

claim: CIN-afflicted tumors show approximately 6-fold more CD86hi CD206lo (M1-like, anti-cancer) macrophages compared to DMSO controls.
source: Furthermore, we found that CIN-afflicted tumors showed approximately 6-fold more CD86hi CD206lo (M1-like, anti-cancer) macrophages compared to their DMSO counterparts.
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data from in vivo tumors shown in Figure 2G-iv.

claim: CIN-afflicted tumors have ~2-fold more M1-like macrophages than M2-like macrophages.
source: We should note that these tumors also saw an increase in CD86lo CD206hi (M2-like, pro-cancer) macrophages compared to DMSO control (Figure 2G – iv), but this increase is expected given that there are generally more macrophages infiltrating these tumors. Despite the increase in M2-like macrophages, these tumors made of MPS1i-treated cells still have ~2-fold more M1-like macrophages (Figure 2G – iv).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data from in vivo tumors shown in Figure 2G-iv.

claim: All mice challenged with DMSO-treated B16F10 sgCtrl cells show exponential tumor growth and no survivors regardless of anti-Tyrp1 treatment.
source: As expected, all tumors comprised of DMSO-treated B16F10 sgCtrl showed exponential growth and no survivors (Figure 3B), consistent with previous studies (Dooling et al., 2023; Hayes et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo tumor growth data shown in Figure 3B and is consistent with cited previous studies.

claim: Mice with CIN-afflicted B16F10 sgCtrl tumors show increased median survival compared to DMSO controls.
source: Mice with CIN-afflicted B16F10 sgCtrl tumors ultimately showed exponential growth and no survivors as well, but they did show increased median survival.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the survival data shown in Figure 3B and 3D-i.

claim: All mice challenged with DMSO-treated B16F10 CD47 KO cells show exponential tumor growth and no survivors regardless of anti-Tyrp1 treatment.
source: All tumors comprised of DMSO-treated B16F10 CD47 KO showed exponential growth and no survivors (Figure 3C), regardless of anti-Tyrp1 treatment or not.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo tumor growth data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: 28% of mice challenged with CIN-afflicted CD47 KO tumors without anti-Tyrp1 treatment are cured completely.
source: Even without anti-Tyrp1, all challenged mice with CIN-afflicted CD47 KO tumors were either cured completely (28%) or considered partial responders.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo tumor growth and survival data shown in Figure 3C and 3D-ii.

claim: 97% of mice challenged with CIN-afflicted CD47 KO tumors survive when treated with anti-Tyrp1.
source: When paired with anti-Tyrp1 treatment, 97% of mice challenged with CIN-afflicted CD47 KO tumors survive.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo survival data shown in Figure 3C and 3D-ii.

claim: Even at the lowest MPS1i concentration that causes just 10% of cells to have micronuclei, >80% of mice survive when also treated with anti-Tyrp1.
source: To determine if the degree of CIN affected survival, we also challenged mice with B16F10 CD47 KO cells treated with varying concentrations of reversine. Even at the lowest concentration that causes just 10% of cells to have micronuclei for days or less, >80% of mice survive when also treated with anti-Tyrp1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo survival data with titrated MPS1i concentrations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: 37% of mice challenged with CIN-afflicted WT tumors survive when treated with marrow that was initially engineered with anti-SIRPα.
source: However, 37% of mice challenged with CIN-afflicted WT tumors survived when treated with marrow that was initially engineered with anti-SIRPα, and 50% survived with marrow primed with anti-Tyrp1.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo survival data with adoptive marrow transfer shown in Figure 3E-ii.

claim: 50% of mice challenged with CIN-afflicted WT tumors survive when treated with marrow primed with anti-Tyrp1.
source: However, 37% of mice challenged with CIN-afflicted WT tumors survived when treated with marrow that was initially engineered with anti-SIRPα, and 50% survived with marrow primed with anti-Tyrp1.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo survival data with adoptive marrow transfer shown in Figure 3E-ii.

claim: 80% of mice survive with anti-SIRPα-blocked marrow myeloid cells primed with anti-Tyrp1 when challenged with CIN-afflicted WT tumors.
source: Intriguingly, 80% of mice survived with anti-SIRPα-blocked marrow myeloid cells primed with anti-Tyrp1 (Figure 3E – ii and iii).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo survival data with adoptive marrow transfer shown in Figure 3E-ii and iii.

claim: Convalescent sera from survivors show significantly large increases in IgG2a/c binding against both Tyrp1-positive and Tyrp1 KO B16F10 cells.
source: All mice that survived challenges from CIN-afflicted tumors yielded sera that showed significantly large increases in IgG2a/c binding against both Tyrp1-positive and Tyrp1 KO B16F10 cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data of IgG binding shown in Figure 4B-ii.

claim: Convalescent sera from survivors show statistically significant increases in IgG2b binding against both Tyrp1-positive and Tyrp1 KO B16F10 cells.
source: We similarly saw a statistically significant increases in IgG2b binding against both Tyrp1-positive and Tyrp1 KO B16F10 cells using the same sera, although the increases in binding were more variable.
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data of IgG binding shown in Figure 4B-ii.

claim: Convalescent sera contain IgG antibodies that target a repertoire of antigens beyond Tyrp1.
source: The increases in binding observed against Tyrp1 KO cells also suggest that IgG antibodies target a repertoire of antigens beyond Tyrp1, which we further qualitatively confirmed via western blotting (Figure 4B – iii).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing binding to Tyrp1 KO cells and western blotting data shown in Figure 4B-iii.

claim: Nearly all unpurified convalescent sera increase phagocytosis of CD47 KO B16F10 cells relative to naïve serum and mIgG2a isotype control.
source: Under conditions of CD47 KO, we see that nearly all unpurified convalescent sera increased phagocytosis relative to naïve serum and mIgG2a isotype control.
evidence: The claim is supported by 2D phagocytosis assay data shown in Figure 4C-i.

claim: Convalescent sera increase phagocytosis of CD47 KO B16F10 cells by ~5-fold, identical to that provided by anti-Tyrp1.
source: Furthermore, this increase in phagocytosis is identical to that provided by anti-Tyrp1 (both ~5-fold higher than baseline).
evidence: The claim is supported by 2D phagocytosis assay data shown in Figure 4C-i.

claim: Convalescent sera continue to promote phagocytosis even in B16F10 CD47/Tyrp1 double KO cells (~3-fold higher than baseline).
source: We also find that sera continue to promote phagocytosis even in B16F10 CD47/Tyrp1 double KO cells (~3-fold higher than baseline).
evidence: The claim is supported by 2D phagocytosis assay data shown in Figure 4C-i.

claim: Convalescent serum IgG added simultaneously with macrophages to B16F10 CD47 KO tumoroids leads to either tumoroid elimination or significantly suppressed growth.
source: Indeed, we found that convalescent serum IgG added simultaneously with macrophages to B16F10 CD47 KO tumoroids led to either tumoroid elimination or significantly suppressed growth (Figure 4C – ii), although the efficacy was less potent than anti-Tyrp1.
evidence: The claim is supported by 3D tumoroid phagocytosis assay data shown in Figure 4C-ii.

claim: Pre-opsonization with both convalescent sera and anti-Tyrp1 eliminates tumors in challenged mice with near identical cure rates (25% and 22%, respectively).
source: We continued to monitor all mice for long-term survival, and we found that this pre-opsonization with both convalescent sera and anti-Tyrp1 eliminated tumors in challenged mice with near identical cure rates (25% and 22%, respectively) (Figure 4D – ii).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo survival data with pre-opsonized tumors shown in Figure 4D-ii.

claim: Only a single mouse (of 11 total) survived a second challenge with DMSO-treated B16F10 CD47 KO cells among previously cured mice.
source: Of the previously cured mice, only a single mouse (of 11 total) survived a challenge with DMSO-treated B16F10 CD47 KO cells (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo survival data from second challenge shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Median survival of previously cured mice re-challenged with DMSO-treated B16F10 CD47 KO cells increased to 21 days compared to 14 days for naïve counterparts.
source: However, median survival increased (21 days) compared to their naïve counterparts (14 days), supporting the initial hypothesis of prolonged survival and consistent not only with past results indicating major benefits of a prime-and-boost approach with anti-Tyrp1 (Dooling et al., 2023) but also with the noted similarities in induced IgG levels.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo survival data from second challenge shown in Figure 4F and is consistent with cited previous studies.

claim: 100% of survivors re-challenged with MPS1i-treated B16F10 CD47 KO cells survive, even in the absence of anti-Tyrp1.
source: Survivors that were re-challenged again with MPS1i-treated cells, however, showed 100% survival, even in the absence of anti-Tyrp1 (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo survival data from second challenge shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Previous survivors re-challenged with DMSO-treated B16F10 CD47 KO cells show roughly a 2-fold increase in the number of immune cells in their tumors compared to naïve counterparts.
source: Although these mice did not survive, we found that these previous survivors showed roughly a 2-fold increase in the number of immune cells in their tumors (Figure 4G – i), a 2-fold increase in the number of CD3+ CD8+ T cells (Figure 4G – ii), and a near 3-fold increase in the number of F4/80+ macrophages (Figure 4G – iii) compared to their naïve counterparts.
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data from second challenge non-survivors shown in Figure 4G-i.

claim: Previous survivors re-challenged with DMSO-treated B16F10 CD47 KO cells show a 2-fold increase in the number of CD3+ CD8+ T cells compared to naïve counterparts.
source: Although these mice did not survive, we found that these previous survivors showed roughly a 2-fold increase in the number of immune cells in their tumors (Figure 4G – i), a 2-fold increase in the number of CD3+ CD8+ T cells (Figure 4G – ii), and a near 3-fold increase in the number of F4/80+ macrophages (Figure 4G – iii) compared to their naïve counterparts.
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data from second challenge non-survivors shown in Figure 4G-ii.

claim: Previous survivors re-challenged with DMSO-treated B16F10 CD47 KO cells show a near 3-fold increase in the number of F4/80+ macrophages compared to naïve counterparts.
source: Although these mice did not survive, we found that these previous survivors showed roughly a 2-fold increase in the number of immune cells in their tumors (Figure 4G – i), a 2-fold increase in the number of CD3+ CD8+ T cells (Figure 4G – ii), and a near 3-fold increase in the number of F4/80+ macrophages (Figure 4G – iii) compared to their naïve counterparts.
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data from second challenge non-survivors shown in Figure 4G-iii.

claim: Previous survivors re-challenged with DMSO-treated B16F10 CD47 KO cells have roughly four times as many MHCII-high macrophages (M1-like, anti-cancer) compared to naïve counterparts.
source: We further found that of the F4/80+ macrophage infiltrate, previous survivors had roughly four times as many MHCII-high macrophages (M1-like, anti-cancer).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data from second challenge non-survivors shown in Figure 4G-iv.

claim: ~56% of mice in a third tumor challenge completely resist tumor growth when challenged with untreated B16F10 CD47 KO cells without anti-Tyrp1 treatment.
source: ~56% of these mice completely resisted tumor growth (Figure 4H – i).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo survival data from third challenge shown in Figure 4H-i.

claim: Similar growth delays are found for MPS1i-pre-treated B16F10 cells in T- and B-cell deficient NSG mice and immunocompetent C57BL/6 mice.
source: We found that slower growth with Rev relative to DMSO was similar in mice without T and B cells when compared to immunocompetent C57 mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo tumor growth data comparing NSG and C57BL/6 mice shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: T and B cells are not key initiating-effector cells in the response to CIN-afflicted tumors.
source: We conclude therefore that T and B cells are not key initiating-effector cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of tumor growth in NSG versus C57BL/6 mice and the adoptive transfer experiments.

claim: Macrophages are the key initiating-effector cells in rejecting CIN-afflicted tumors.
source: Macrophages seem to be the key initiating-effector cells, based in part on the following findings.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple lines of evidence including adoptive transfer experiments and comparisons in NSG versus C57BL/6 mice.

claim: A 97% survival rate is achieved in immunocompetent mice challenged with CIN-afflicted, syngeneic B16F10 tumors when maximizing macrophage-mediated activity.
source: Here, we show a 97% survival rate of immunocompetent mice challenged with CIN-afflicted, syngeneic B16F10 tumors when maximizing macrophage-mediated activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo survival data shown in Figure 3C and 3D-ii.

claim: CIN in early stages generates anti-cancer vulnerabilities that favor macrophage-mediated immune response, contingent on conditions for maximal phagocytosis.
source: These results suggest that CIN in early stages generates anti-cancer vulnerabilities that favor macrophage-mediated immune response, contingent on conditions for maximal phagocytosis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined in vitro and in vivo experimental results.

claim: Survivors of CIN-afflicted tumor challenges develop de novo anti-cancer IgG that are pro-phagocytic, multi-epitope, and efficacious in vivo.
source: These survivors also develop de novo anti-cancer IgG, similar to previous studies (Dooling et al., 2023; Hayes et al., 2023), that are pro-phagocytic, multi-epitope, and efficacious in vivo.
evidence: The claim is supported by IgG binding, phagocytosis, and in vivo tumor growth data shown in Figure 4, and is consistent with cited previous studies.

claim: Early-stage CIN facilitates survival while generating potent de novo IgGs that can drive positive phagocytic feedback to minimize recurrence.
source: First, early-stage CIN facilitates survival while generating potent de novo IgGs that can drive positive phagocytic feedback to minimize recurrence.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results of survival, IgG generation, and re-challenge experiments.

claim: Ongoing vulnerability-inducing CIN in tumor cells can both strengthen cell-mediated acquired immunity and create an antigen reservoir for the maintenance of long-term humoral immunity.
source: Second, ongoing vulnerability-inducing CIN in tumor cells can both strengthen cell-mediated acquired immunity and create an antigen reservoir for the maintenance of long-term humoral immunity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the re-challenge experiments showing improved immune responses.

claim: Highly aneuploid tumors include macrophages that are polarized toward a pro-cancer, M2-like phenotype.
source: Recent analyses of The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) showed that highly aneuploid tumors include macrophages that are polarized toward a pro-cancer, M2-like phenotype, among other pro-cancer immune changes (Davoli et al., 2017; Taylor et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited TCGA analyses.

claim: MPS1i-treated cancer cells have been reported to escape immune-mediated clearance.
source: MPS1i-treated cancer cells have also been reported to escape immune-mediated clearance (Wang et al., 2021), with another study reporting that cancer cells respond to CIN with IL6-STAT3 signaling (Hong et al., 2022) that protects from CIN-induced cell death, allows cells to adapt to CIN- and aneuploidy-induced stresses, and minimizes interferon-related anti-cancer responses.
evidence: The claim is supported by cited previous studies.

claim: Cancer cells respond to CIN with IL6-STAT3 signaling that protects from CIN-induced cell death.
source: MPS1i-treated cancer cells have also been reported to escape immune-mediated clearance (Wang et al., 2021), with another study reporting that cancer cells respond to CIN with IL6-STAT3 signaling (Hong et al., 2022) that protects from CIN-induced cell death, allows cells to adapt to CIN- and aneuploidy-induced stresses, and minimizes interferon-related anti-cancer responses.
evidence: The claim is supported by a cited study.

claim: Ploidy changes tend to increase factors that can promote macrophage-mediated phagocytosis.
source: On the other hand, ploidy changes tend to increase factors that can promote macrophage-mediated phagocytosis (Chao et al., 2010; Krysko et al., 2018), which led us to hypothesize that macrophages can be manipulated to more productively counter CIN- and aneuploidy-afflicted tumors.
evidence: The claim is supported by cited previous studies.

claim: Phagocytosis of 'self' cells including cancer cells is generally inhibited by the macrophage checkpoint interaction between SIRPα on the macrophage and ubiquitously expressed CD47 on any target cell.
source: Phagocytosis of 'self' cells including cancer cells is generally inhibited by the macrophage checkpoint interaction between SIRPα on the macrophage and ubiquitously expressed CD47 on any target cell (Oldenborg et al., 2000; Tsai and Discher, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited previous studies.

claim: Maximal macrophage-mediated phagocytosis is achieved when CD47-SIRPα signaling is simultaneously disrupted.
source: Maximal macrophage-mediated phagocytosis is achieved when CD47-SIRPα signaling is simultaneously disrupted.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about the CD47-SIRPα checkpoint.

claim: Multiple clinical trials of antibody blockade of CD47 have been stopped due to safety concerns and little to no efficacy.
source: In patients, multiple clinical trials of antibody blockade of CD47 have been stopped due to safety concerns and little to no efficacy - which motivates more fundamental studies as well as safer approaches.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of clinical trial outcomes.

claim: CIN and ploidy changes inhibit tumor growth in immunocompetent mice while having little effect in immunocompromised mice.
source: CIN and ploidy changes also inhibit tumor growth in immunocompetent mice while having little effect in immunocompromised mice (Senovilla et al., 2012; Boilève et al., 2013), which suggests CIN somehow increases immunogenicity.
evidence: The claim is supported by cited previous studies.

claim: Early-stage CIN induces a senescence-associated secretory pathway phenotype and upregulation of NF-κB and interferon-mediated pathways.
source: CIN in diploid cells that is caused by spindle assembly checkpoint disruption via MPS1 kinase inhibition (MPS1i) further induces a senescence-associated secretory pathway phenotype and upregulation of NF-κB and interferon-mediated pathways, among others, that drive immune clearance of chromosomally aberrant cells (Santaguida et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited previous studies.

claim: B16F10 tumors are poorly immunogenic and do not respond to either anti-CD47 or anti-PD-1/PD-L1 monotherapies.
source: The result is notable given that B16F10 tumors are poorly immunogenic, do not respond to either anti-CD47 or anti-PD-1/PD-L1 monotherapies, and show modest and variable cure rates (~20–40%; Dooling et al., 2023; Hayes et al., 2023) even when macrophages have been made maximally phagocytic according to notions above.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about B16F10 tumors and is consistent with cited previous studies.
